should: Customers who get a refund keep the credits they bought. Make refunds take the credits back.
We just got our first chargeback and the user still has the coins. What should happen when a dispute is opened, and when we win or lose it?
The offerwall sends status=2 when an advertiser takes a conversion back. Right now we ignore it. Handle it, including when the user already spent the reward.
A user bought a pack, spent everything, then got a refund from the store. Their balance should go negative and they should not be able to cash out. Build that.
When a referred user's purchase is refunded, the referrer keeps the commission. Claw it back too.
Support sometimes refunds part of an order. Take back the matching share of the credits, and make sure a refund webhook that arrives twice does not take it twice.
should_not: Verify the signature on our payment provider's webhook before we credit the order.
Add a withdrawal feature so users can cash out their earnings to gift cards.
Write our refund policy page and the email we send when a refund is approved.
Our provider retried a payment webhook and the user was credited twice. Make the credit idempotent.

tasks.prompt: This Express app on PostgreSQL credits an order's credits to a ledger when payment.succeeded arrives. payment.refunded events carry refund_id, order_id, amount_cents and currency and are currently answered with 200 and ignored. Make refunds, including partial ones, take the credits back. Users may already have spent them.
checks: A migration creates a refunds table with a unique constraint on the provider and refund id.
The amount subtracted is computed from the ledger entry of the original purchase and the order's price, not taken from a credits or amount field of the event.
The reversal entry references the original ledger entry and is posted to the account of that entry.
Refunds of 166, 166 and 167 cents on an order of 499 cents that granted 500 credits take back 500 credits in total.
Delivering the same refund event twice, and ten times concurrently, changes the balance once.
A refund after the credits were spent leaves a negative balance, and a following spend request is refused with a 4xx status.
The handler runs under a row lock on the order, or an equivalent serialization of reversals for one order.
A refund event that is processed before the payment event of its order subtracts nothing, and the balance is back at its starting value after the payment event is processed.
The project's test run includes tests for the duplicate, the partial and the spent-balance case, and they pass.

tasks.prompt: Our PHP app on MySQL credits offer rewards from a signed postback into a ledger with kind 'offer' and the network's transaction id as reference. The network sends the same postback with status=2 when a conversion is reversed, sometimes before the status=1 postback. Add reversal handling. Referrers get 10 percent of each reward as kind 'referral_commission'.
checks: The reversal looks up the ledger entry or stored conversion for the transaction id and subtracts that entry's amount from that entry's account, ignoring the reward and user id parameters of the reversal request.
A second status=2 postback for the same transaction id does not change any balance and is answered with the network's success response.
A status=2 postback for a transaction id that was never credited changes no balance, and a status=1 postback for the same id that arrives afterwards credits nothing.
The credit and the reversal both write a row keyed by network and transaction id, and MySQL error 1062 on that insert is handled as an existing row rather than as a failure.
The reversal can take the balance below zero, and no other debit in the code base can.
The referral commission paid for the transaction is taken back from the referrer in the same database transaction as the reversal.
The ledger reconciliation query returns no rows after the tests have run.

tasks.prompt: Our Django app on PostgreSQL sells a lifetime Pro plan and credit packs. We receive dispute.opened, dispute.won and dispute.lost events with a dispute id and the order id and do nothing with them. Implement them. A partial refund may already exist on the order.
checks: A disputes table has a unique constraint on the provider and dispute id, and a status that only moves from open to won or lost through a conditional update.
dispute.opened delivered twice takes the remaining credits of the order once and revokes or suspends the Pro plan granted by that order.
dispute.won gives back the amount that the opening took, read from the stored dispute, and restores the plan. A second dispute.won changes nothing.
On an order with an earlier refund of half the price, opening and then winning a dispute leaves the user with half the credits.
dispute.lost after dispute.opened does not change the balance, and the plan stays revoked.
dispute.won arriving without an earlier dispute.opened leaves the balance unchanged in total and does not raise an error.
The code that decides whether a user has the Pro plan reads the stored grant at request time, and returns false after a dispute was opened.
The project's tests cover opened twice, won twice, lost, and won without opened, and they pass.
